title: Hypertrophy training is CANCELLED
summary: Responding to Instagram skits by Emanuel and Eugene Teo that mock 'science-based' hypertrophy training, NH argues the problem isn't machines or stable lifts but low effort and an obsession with avoiding fatigue. He defends the Smith machine and the evolution of training methods, says mobility and strength come along with good hypertrophy training, and calls for combining fatiguing compounds with isolation lifts pushed to failure.
claims: Mocking hypertrophy training through the iliac pulldown is a strawman; proper hypertrophy training should be mostly heavy compound movements taken to failure
The barbell pullover, drag curl and sissy squat are good bodybuilding lifts, not strength lifts
Classic hypertrophy staples from 100 years ago are still relevant but have fallen out of favour because of science hype around shinier lifts
For hypertrophy, do one-arm dumbbell presses with an upright torso, straight legs, a pause and a slow tempo; twisting the torso is a strength technique for moving more weight
Bodybuilders should prefer dumbbells and a slow negative on triceps extensions for stability and size
Most movements need high stability to be optimal for hypertrophy
Without proximity to failure and real effort every movement gives poor hypertrophy, however well it recruits fibres
The iliac pulldown is a noob trap: it is easy and needs no technical adaptation, so beginners choose it over harder, more productive lifts like dumbbell rows and pull-ups
Lifts that take a long time to learn often pay off with a higher rate and range of progression than lifts you are good at immediately
Beginners on high-rep machine work tend to sandbag; by rep 8 of a 15-rep set most stop pushing, while a 3RM forces full effort
Once you know how to push, a 15-rep max on a Smith incline press is excellent for hypertrophy; free weights and machines are equally effective with different benefits
Straps on back work don't hurt forearm development; they let you isolate the back better, and letting grip limit back growth leaves gains on the table
Combined lifts like the hip-thrust-to-floor-press make no sense, because the weight is right for only one of the two movements
Risky stunt lifts with a poor risk-to-reward ratio have no place in a bodybuilding program
Fitness should evolve; training exactly as people did 100 years ago would mean the field had failed
Natural lifters today are bigger and stronger than in the past thanks to better methods and technology
Jack LaLanne invented the Smith machine to get barbell training without free-weight risk; mocking it shows ignorance of fitness history
The 'useless muscle' talk of functional training is propaganda; a muscle trained through a function will do that function
Mobility can and should be gained through hypertrophy training, by loading muscles through full ranges of motion
Hypertrophy needs full range of motion and increasing load; your goal is not strength, but you will have to get stronger
Romanian deadlifts, deep pull-ups and deep preacher curls build both mobility and size, and you progress by adding weight and range
Any exercise sold as good for mobility should also be taken to failure and done heavy; extra range of motion lowers the load for you anyway
Today's 'basics' (squat, bench, deadlift) are just the powerlifting meta; every era had different basics, and the pullover was once a staple
Influencers decide which lifts are fashionable; popularity and tradition are poor guides to what builds muscle
Lifts now considered best for hypertrophy share two traits: high stability and a high stimulus-to-fatigue ratio
Leg curls have a better stimulus-to-fatigue ratio than RDLs, but RDLs develop the upper back, traps, glutes and lower back too; someone doing only leg curls ends up weaker and smaller
Pull-ups give more overall back and arm stimulus but stress the elbow, biceps and shoulders more; the iliac pulldown targets lats with little wear
Use big compounds and precise isolations together: compounds alone risk imbalances and overuse injuries, while isolations alone build much less overall size
Modern hypertrophy culture leans too far toward low-fatigue, ultra-stable lifts and dismisses anything less stable
Incline curls on a slight incline are excellent; a near-horizontal incline makes the bottom too hard and the top too easy, which spoils progression
For a big biceps stretch with constant tension, use Bayesian cable curls instead of very deep incline curls
Isolation lifts have the best stimulus-to-fatigue ratio and should be pushed hardest, to failure and with rest-pause, not done light for the pump
Heavy compounds benefit more from leaving reps in reserve because each rep gives so much stimulus and fatigue
The iliac pulldown should be taken to failure and done hard; it is hated because of the light, slow, high-rep way it was promoted, not because of the movement
